newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Goh warns on property overbuilding.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Goh warns on property overbuilding.

text.p: Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said on Wednesday that overbuilding could lead to a property market collapse.

"If we overbuild properties to satisfy get-rich-quick demand fanned by low interest rates, easy credit and expectation of big capital gains, the property market may collapse, causing serious problems for the whole economy," Goh said in a May Day message.
Singapore took steps earlier in the month to tighten credit rules for government-subsidised housing, moves which had a ripple effect on the island state's private property market.
This week, property shares on the Stock Exchange of Singapore have been under heavy selling pressure from talk that further curbs were to be announced at a weekend news conference.
However, a Ministry of National Development spokesman said on Tuesday he was aware of no plans for a news conference this week.
Goh's comments on the property market were among several warnings he issued about the dangers mature economies face.
Noting economic problems in Europe, Goh said: "We cannot assume that high growth and the good life will last forever."
Wage increases had to be matched by productivity growth, Goh said.
"Nominal wage increases will either be eroded by high inflation and a depreciating Singapore dollar, or else will result in higher unemployment."

Goh stressed the need for education and worker training, and said Singapore's political stability was a plus in attracting international investment. Goh's People's Action Party has ruled Singapore since 1959.
Despite a slowdown in the electronic sector in 1996, Goh said the revolution in electronics and information was far from over.
"Hence, unless we foolishly throw away our competitive advantage, we will enjoy the immense benefits of a growth industry," he said.
Singapore's full year overall economic growth for 1996 was seven percent, significantly below the 8.8 percent expansion of 1995 and the double-digit growth of the previous two years.
